subsection: 2. Role, status, socio-economic groupings, social mobility

notes.b: Everyone occupies positions in society, and each position carries a certain standing in other people's eyes. Sociologists call such a position a status, and one person holds several at the same time.
points: A status is a social position, such as mother, teacher, employee or citizen. One person holds several at once, for example daughter, student, goalkeeper and citizen, so a status describes one part of who a person is, not the whole person.
An ascribed status is given at birth or without choice, for example sex, age, ethnic origin or the family into which a person is born.
An achieved status is gained through effort, choice or ability, for example a qualification, a job or a marriage.

Being a parent or a spouse is usually treated as achieved because it follows from choices a person makes. Social class at birth is ascribed, but class in adulthood is mostly achieved through occupation.
A master status is a status that dominates how others see a person and outweighs the person's other statuses, for example being a serving prisoner.
Status can be based on occupation, education, wealth, family background or achievement. In a society that rewards achievement a person can raise their status, which links directly to social mobility.
Societies that allocate status mainly by birth are described as closed; societies that allocate it mainly by achievement are described as open.
notes.tip: Status and role are not synonyms: status is the position a person holds, role is the behaviour expected of them. Also remember that being a parent or spouse is usually treated as achieved, while sex, age and ethnicity are ascribed.

notes.b: A status tells you where a person stands; a role tells you how they are expected to behave there. Roles are learned through socialisation (the process of learning the ways of a society).
points: A role is the set of behaviours and expectations attached to a status: the rights, duties and behaviour considered appropriate for a person according to their position in society. Examples include teacher, student, adult, child and parent.

Status and role go together. A teacher (the status) is expected to prepare lessons, mark work and treat pupils fairly (the role). Likewise, the role of a student includes attending class, completing homework and respecting the teacher.
A person plays many roles at once, such as mother, employee, daughter and club member.

Roles change over the life course: a person moves from the role of child to adolescent to adult, and each stage brings different expectations. They also change over time, for example gender roles within the family.
Role conflict occurs when the demands of two roles are incompatible, so meeting one means failing the other.
For example, a parent who is also a manager is asked to work late when a child is ill, or a person is expected to be both a loyal friend and an honest employee.

Role overload occurs when a person has too many roles and cannot meet all the demands placed on them, which reduces leisure time and increases stress. For example, a working parent also cares for an elderly relative.
Role conflict and role overload are most common where people hold several demanding roles at once.
A role model is a person whose behaviour others copy, such as a parent, teacher or sports star.
notes.tip: Keep the two terms apart: role conflict is a clash between two roles with incompatible demands, while role overload is simply too many roles to cope with. If a question asks for both, define each separately with its own example, because each point is credited separately.

notes.b: People in a society are not all in the same economic and social position. Socio-economic groups sort people into categories according to that position, and they show that society is arranged in layers.
points: A socio-economic group (also called a social class) is a category of people with a similar economic and social position, defined mainly by occupation and linked to income, education, wealth, housing and lifestyle.
Social stratification is the division of a society into layers, a hierarchy of unequal ranks. A socio-economic scheme is one way of describing those layers.

In Ireland the Central Statistics Office (CSO) groups the population into social classes for the census, using the occupation of each person. The groups run from professional workers, managerial and technical, non-manual, skilled manual and semi-skilled to unskilled, with a further group for all others gainfully occupied and unknown.

Occupation, not education, decides which class a person is placed in, so a qualification affects the class only through the job it leads to. Level of education is one of the strongest factors separating socio-economic groups, because it governs access to skilled and professional work.

Examples of occupations, one per group: doctor or solicitor (professional); manager or technician (managerial and technical); factory worker (semi-skilled); labourer (unskilled). Electrician, plumber, carpenter or motor mechanic are skilled manual occupations.
Factors that determine socio-economic group are occupation, income, education level, wealth, housing and family background.

Socio-economic group affects life chances, meaning a person's likelihood of access to opportunities such as educational attainment, health, housing and income. It also shapes housing choices and household expenditure.

Higher socio-economic groups are more likely to complete second level and go on to third level, while lower groups face higher early school leaving and lower expectations. This affects equality of opportunity in education.
notes.tip: For a definition of socio-economic group, say it is a category of people by economic and social position, based on occupation, income or education, and add an example. A bare definition gets only about half the marks, so always include an everyday example.

notes.b: People do not always stay in the socio-economic group they start in. Social mobility is the movement of an individual or a group between socio-economic groups, enabled by education, income and occupation. It does not mean geographical mobility, which is moving house or country.
points: Upward mobility is movement to a higher socio-economic group, for example a labourer's child who becomes a teacher, or a skilled worker who becomes a manager after completing a degree.
Downward mobility is movement to a lower socio-economic group, for example after the loss of a skilled job with no replacement at the same level.
There are two time frames for measuring social mobility. Intergenerational mobility compares a person's position with the position of their parents.
Intragenerational mobility, sometimes called career mobility, compares a person's position at different points in their own working life, for example from apprentice to manager.

Structural mobility is movement caused by changes in the occupational structure, such as the growth of professional and service jobs and fewer farm jobs, so that many people move even when their relative positions do not change.
Exchange mobility is movement in both directions that balances out, so that the overall pattern of relative positions stays the same.

Factors that help people move up include education and qualifications, skills and training, promotion in a job, a good income, free second-level education, access to third level (grants, free fees schemes), equality legislation, ambition and family support. Education is the main route to upward mobility in Ireland.

Barriers to mobility include low family income, poor access to education and third-level education, early school leaving, discrimination, unemployment and living in an area with few employment opportunities.
Social mobility is more likely in an open society, where status is achieved, than in a closed society, where status is ascribed.
notes.tip: When asked to explain social mobility, define it as movement between socio-economic groups and name education or occupation as the means. Do not confuse it with moving house or country.

keyTerms.definition: A social position a person holds within a group or society.
A status given at birth or without choice, such as sex or family background.
A status gained through effort or choice, such as a qualification or a job.
A status that dominates how others see a person and outweighs their other statuses.
The set of behaviours and expectations attached to a status.
A situation in which the incompatible demands of two roles cannot both be met.
A situation in which a person has too many roles and cannot meet all the demands placed on them.
A category of people grouped by occupation, income, education, wealth and housing.
The division of a society into layers of unequal rank.
The movement of an individual or group between socio-economic groups.
Movement between groups caused by changes in the occupational structure of the economy.
A comparison of a person's socio-economic position with the position of their parents.

factCards.definition: Ascribed status is given at birth or without choice; achieved status is gained through effort or choice.

factCards.term: Two time frames for measuring social mobility
factCards.definition: Intergenerational mobility compares a person with their parents; intragenerational mobility compares a person at different points in their own career.
Low family income, lack of access to third-level education and discrimination.

factCards.term: Three factors that help people move up
factCards.definition: Education and qualifications, skills and training, and access to occupations with promotion prospects.
Role conflict arises when two roles make incompatible demands; role overload arises when a person has too many roles to meet.
Growth or decline of particular occupations as the economy changes, such as the expansion of professional and service jobs.

factCards.term: Example of a skilled manual occupation
factCards.definition: Electrician, plumber, carpenter or motor mechanic.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between ascribed status and achieved status, giving one example of each.
questions.model: Ascribed status is given at birth or without choice, for example sex, ethnic origin or family background. Achieved status is gained through effort or choice, for example a qualification, a job or a marriage.

questions.prompt: Discuss how role conflict and role overload can arise in family and working life, and explain how education can allow a person to move between socio-economic groups.
questions.model: Role conflict arises when the incompatible demands of two roles cannot both be met, for example a parent who is also a manager and is asked to work late when a child is ill. Role overload arises when a person holds too many roles, for example a working parent who also cares for an elderly relative. Socio-economic groups are categories based on occupation, income, education, wealth and housing. Social mobility is the movement of individuals between these groups. Education is a key route to upward mobility because qualifications open access to skilled and professional occupations. Upward mobility is movement to a higher group, for example a skilled worker who becomes a manager after a degree. Structural mobility also results from changes in the occupational structure. Barriers such as low family income and limited access to third-level education can prevent education from producing mobility.
